relationship: Thematic comparison of divine protection of the holy city
rationale: The letter credits God with driving out opponents arrayed against the holy city. The psalm describes God supporting His city while assembled kings are troubled and shaken. Both locate the city's security in God's action against threatening rulers; the psalm is not identified as a prediction or account of this particular expulsion.
source_text: for He Himself drove out those arrayed against us in the holy city.

target_units.text: God is known in her citadels when He supports her.
For behold, the kings gathered; they came together.
They saw and thus marveled; they were troubled and shaken.
Trembling seized them; there were pangs like a woman giving birth.
With a violent wind Thou wilt shatter the ships of Tarshish.
Just as we heard, so we saw in the city of the Lord of powers, in our God’s city; God founded her for ever. Diapsalma.

relationship: Liturgical parallel of a leader and answering assembly
rationale: Jonathan begins the prayer while the priests and others respond during the sacrifice; Esdras blesses the Lord and all the people answer Amen. Both depict public prayer with a leader and a responding congregation. The occasions remain distinct; Maccabees does not specify an Amen response, and Jonathan is not identified with Esdras.
source_text: While the sacrifice was being consumed, the priests offered prayer—the priests and everyone—with Jonathan beginning and the others responding, as Nehemiah did.

target_units.text: Esdras blessed the Lord, the great God. All the people answered and said, “Amen,” lifting their hands, and they bowed and worshiped the Lord with their faces to the ground.

rationale: The priests sing hymns in response after the sacrificial prayer; at the foundation of the Lord's house, priests and Levites participate in answering praise and thanksgiving. The shared practice is responsive temple praise, without identifying the unnamed hymns in Maccabees as Ezra's quoted refrain or equating the ceremonies.
source_text: The priests sang the hymns in response.

target_units.text: They laid the foundation for building the Lord’s house, and the priests stood in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites, sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord according to the directions of David king of Israel.

They answered in praise and thanksgiving to the Lord: “For it is good, for His mercy toward Israel endures for ever.” All the people sounded a great cry of praise to the Lord at the founding of the Lord’s house.

relationship: Archival preservation of royal provisions for sacred gifts
rationale: Nehemiah's reported library includes kings' letters about dedicated gifts. Ezra describes a treasury-library search and a preserved memorandum of Cyrus's provisions for rebuilding the Jerusalem house and returning its gold and silver vessels. Both associate collected written royal records with sacred endowments; Ezra's memorandum is not asserted to be one of Nehemiah's particular letters or in the same archive.
source_text: These same things were related in the records and in the memoirs concerning Nehemiah, and also how, in establishing a library, he gathered together the books concerning the kings and prophets, the writings of David, and kings’ letters concerning dedicated gifts.

target_units.text: Then Darius the king issued a decision and made a search in the libraries where the treasury is kept in Babylon.
A scroll was found in a city, in the citadel of the city of the Medes, and this was written in it: “Memorandum:

In the first year of Cyrus the king, King Cyrus issued a decision concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be built, and the place where they sacrifice the sacrifices. He set an elevation: sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide,
with three courses of strong stone and one wooden course. The expense will be paid from the king’s house.

And let the silver and gold vessels of God’s house, which Nabouchodonosor took from the house in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, be given back and go to the sanctuary in Jerusalem, to the place where they were set in God’s house.”

relationship: Literary reflection on the bodily cost of study and writing
rationale: The abridger describes the work of producing the condensed history as sweat and sleeplessness. Ecclesiastes links the making of many books and much study with weariness of the flesh. Both explicitly connect literary work with bodily strain, while the abridger willingly undertakes the task and Ecclesiastes issues a caution.
source_text: For us who have undertaken the hard work of abridgement, the task is not easy; it involves sweat and sleeplessness.

target_units.text: My son, beware of making many books; there is no limit, and much study is weariness of the flesh.

relationship: Comparison of building metaphors for different responsibilities
rationale: The abridger distinguishes an architect's concern for the whole foundation from the decorator's work to explain historian and abridger roles. Paul distinguishes laying a foundation as a master builder from another person's building upon it. Both use construction roles to distinguish responsibilities; Paul's foundation is explicitly Jesus Christ, and the literary historian is not equated with that foundation.
source_text: For just as the architect of a new house must consider its whole foundation, while the person undertaking its encaustic work and painting must examine what is suitable for decoration, so, I think, it is with us.

target_units.text: According to the grace of God given to me, I laid a foundation as a wise master builder, and another builds upon it. But let each one watch how he builds upon it.
For no one can lay another foundation besides the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

relationship: Visible facial distress revealing inner sorrow
rationale: Onias's changed face reveals the anguish of his soul to observers. The king reads the speaker's distressed face as distress of heart, and the speaker explains his grief over the devastated city. Both make facial appearance an outward sign of inward sorrow; the threatened temple deposits and the burned city gates are different causes.
source_text: Whoever saw the high priest’s appearance was wounded in mind, for his face and altered complexion revealed his soul’s anguish.

target_units.text: The king said to me, “Why is your face distressed when you are not unwell? This is nothing but distress of heart.” I became very greatly afraid.
I said to the king, “May the king live for ever! Why should my face not be distressed, since the city, the home of my fathers’ tombs, has been laid waste and its gates have been consumed by fire?”

rationale: People leave their houses for public supplication because the sanctuary is threatened with contempt, while the priests plead in the surrounding scene. Joel calls the congregation together and has the priests ask that God's inheritance not be given to reproach or foreign rule. Both present communal assembly and priestly petition against disgrace, without treating Heliodorus's mission as the fulfilment of Joel's summons.
source_text: People also rushed out of their houses in crowds for a public supplication, because the place was about to be treated with contempt.

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service.
Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

relationship: Sacrifice and vows after danger to life
rationale: Heliodorus sacrifices and makes vows to the One who preserved his life after his near-fatal ordeal. Jonah recalls his failing life and promises thankful sacrifice and repayment of his vows while praying for deliverance. Both connect endangered life, appeal to the Lord, sacrifice and vows; Heliodorus's enacted offering and Jonah's promised offering remain distinct.
source_text: Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made very great vows to the One who had preserved his life. He warmly took leave of Onias and departed with his company to the king.

target_units.text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.
Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.
But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

rationale: The priests in Maccabees despise the temple and neglect its sacrifices in favour of athletic exercises. Malachi rebukes priests who belittle God's name and treat His table as despised by bringing polluted and defective offerings. Both condemn priests' contempt for their altar responsibilities, with neglect for athletics distinguished from the presentation of unacceptable offerings.
source_text: that the priests were no longer eager for the services of the altar. Despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful provision of exercises in the wrestling ground after the signal for the discus.

target_units.text: “A son honors his father, and a slave his master. If I am a father, where is My honor? If I am a master, where is the fear of Me?” says the Lord Almighty. You priests who belittle My name! But you said, “How have we belittled Thy name?”
“By bringing polluted loaves to My altar.” But you said, “How have we polluted them?” “By your saying, ‘The Lord’s table is despised, and the foods placed upon it are despised.’”

“For if you bring a blind animal for sacrifice, is that not evil? If you bring one that is lame or sick, is that not evil? Bring it, then, to your ruler! Will he accept it? Will he show you favor?” says the Lord Almighty.

relationship: Royal mourning for a man unjustly killed
rationale: Antiochus weeps over Onias after learning of his unjust murder and admiring his conduct. David leads mourning for Abner, weeps at his grave and laments his fall before men of injustice. Both narratives show a king grieving an unjust killing, without equating the victims, their offices or the kings' later treatment of the killers.
source_text: Antiochus was deeply grieved, moved to pity, and wept because of the deceased man’s self-restraint and admirable conduct.

target_units.text: David said to Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your garments, put on sackcloth, and beat yourselves in mourning before Abner.” King David walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king lifted his voice and wept at his grave, and all the people wept over Abner.
The king lamented over Abner and said, “Should Abner die according to Nabal’s death?
Your hands were not bound; your feet were not in fetters. He did not bring near, as Nabal; before men of injustice you fell.” All the people gathered to weep over him.

relationship: Loss of mourning and honourable burial
rationale: Jason, who left others unburied, receives neither mourning nor funeral care or an ancestral tomb. Jeremiah announces that Jehoiakim will not be mourned and will receive a dishonourable burial outside Jerusalem's gate. Both portray deprivation of mourning and proper burial as an ignominious end, without identifying Jason with Jehoiakim or assigning the same disposal of the body to both.
source_text: He who had thrown out multitudes unburied went unmourned and received neither any funeral care whatever nor a place in his ancestral tomb.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!
He will be buried with a donkey’s burial; swept up, he will be thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate.

relationship: Comparison of lists describing slaughter across age and sex
rationale: The massacre narrative lists young and old, women, children, virgins and infants among those killed. Ezekiel's vision similarly lists old men, young men, maidens, infants and women in the order to strike Jerusalem. The shared enumeration conveys the breadth of the killing; the vision explicitly exempts those bearing the sign, and Antiochus's soldiers are not identified with its agents or granted its divine commission.
source_text: There was killing of young and old, destruction of boys, women and children, and slaughter of virgins and infants.

target_units.text: To these others He said while I listened, “Go behind him into the city and strike. Do not spare with your eyes, and have no mercy.

Old man, young man, maiden, infants and women—kill them to obliteration. But do not approach anyone upon whom the sign is. Begin at My holy places.” They began with the elderly men who were inside the house.

relationship: Wisdom principle linking honourable age and righteousness
rationale: Eleazar judges his resolve by the dignity of old age and his lifelong excellent conduct, with God's law foremost. Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in ways of righteousness. The narrative embodies the connection between honourable age and righteous conduct; the proverb does not name Eleazar or prescribe his particular martyrdom.
source_text: But he adopted a noble resolve, worthy of his age, the dignity of his old age, his acquired and distinguished gray hair, his excellent conduct from childhood, and still more the holy legislation established by God. Accordingly he declared at once that they should send him to Hades.

target_units.text: Old age is a crown of boasting, and it is found in ways of righteousness.

relationship: Wisdom principle of conduct fitting gray hair
rationale: Eleazar's resolve is described as worthy of his age and distinguished gray hair alongside his excellent conduct from childhood. Sirach calls judgment, wisdom and counsel fitting for gray hair and elders, and names fear of the Lord their boast. Both link the honour of age to moral and discerning conduct, without claiming Sirach describes Eleazar's biography or commands his particular decision.
source_text: But he adopted a noble resolve, worthy of his age, the dignity of his old age, his acquired and distinguished gray hair, his excellent conduct from childhood, and still more the holy legislation established by God. Accordingly he declared at once that they should send him to Hades.

target_units.text: How fitting is judgment for gray hair, and knowledge of counsel for elders!
How fitting is wisdom for the old, and thought and counsel for the honored!
Long experience is the crown of the old, and their boast is the fear of the Lord.
